examples.label: Confirm you're in a medium-integrity admin context

notes:
=== UAC Overview and Enumeration ===
UAC is a convenience feature, NOT a security boundary. It restricts admin tokens by default.

=== HOW UAC WORKS ===
Admin accounts get TWO tokens at logon:
1. Standard user token (used by default at medium integrity)
2. Full administrator token (used only when elevation is granted)
RID 500 built-in Administrator is EXEMPT from UAC - always operates at high integrity.
All other admin accounts run at medium integrity unless elevated.

=== ENUMERATION ===
EnableLUA value:
  reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\NT\CurrentVersion\UAC" /v EnableLUA
  0x0 = UAC disabled entirely (auto-elevate everything)
  0x1 = UAC enabled

ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin (controls prompt behavior):
  reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\NT\CurrentVersion\UAC" /v ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin
  0x0 = no prompt, auto-elevate
  0x1 = prompt for credentials (no prompt on secure desktop)
  0x2 = prompt for consent (non-Windows binaries only)
  0x5 = Always notify (hardest to bypass - fewest techniques work)

Windows build version (cross-reference against UACME bypass list):
  [environment]::OSVersion.Version

=== DECISION FLOW ===
Is current token high integrity?
  Yes → UAC already bypassed or not needed
  No → Is UAC enabled (EnableLUA=1)?
       No → running as medium but policies may still restrict
       Yes → select bypass technique based on build + ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin level

=== CHAINING CONTEXT ===
UAC bypass is a PREREQUISITE step when:
- Account is in local Administrators group but operating with restricted token
- Need SeDebugPrivilege, SeLoadDriverPrivilege, or other privileges stripped by UAC
- Preparing for LSASS dump, Capcom exploit, or any privilege-requiring technique
After bypass: full admin token unlocks all privilege-based escalation paths

=== UACME REFERENCE ===
https://github.com/hfiref0x/UACME catalogs techniques by build number, binary, patch status
Always check build number before selecting technique to avoid wasting time on patched methods

recommended.note: Bypass UAC via the srrstr.dll hijack.

name: UAC - Enumerate Configuration
description: Confirm UAC is on and read its level before choosing a bypass. EnableLUA=1 means UAC active; ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin sets the prompt strictness. The OS build number determines which bypass works.

defense.why_it_works: Registry keys EnableLUA and ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin reveal the UAC configuration. EnableLUA=0 means UAC is entirely disabled (all processes run as full admin without elevation prompts). ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin values 0-3 indicate auto-elevation or silent elevation configurations that are bypassable. This reconnaissance step identifies whether UAC bypass is needed or if admin is already available.
defense.prerequisites: Shell access. Read access to HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System registry key.
defense.impact: Reconnaissance - identifies whether UAC is disabled (immediate admin access) or misconfigured (bypassable), informing attack path selection.
defense.detection: reg query on System policy key by standard user. PowerShell Get-ItemProperty on UAC registry path. SIEM: UAC configuration query.
defense.artifacts: Process log: reg query HKLM\...\Policies\System by standard user
defense.splunk_spl:
index=sysmon EventCode=1 Image="*reg.exe" CommandLine="*Policies\\System*EnableLUA*"
| table _time, Computer, User, CommandLine
defense.elastic_kql: event.code:"1" AND process.name:reg.exe AND process.command_line:(*Policies\\System* AND *EnableLUA*)
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "EnableLUA"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
defense.prevention: Keep UAC enabled (EnableLUA=1). Set ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=2 (always prompt for credentials). Enable PowerShell logging to detect reconnaissance. Educate administrators on UAC importance.
defense.misconfiguration: UAC disabled entirely (EnableLUA=0) for convenience. UAC set to auto-elevate without prompting (ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=0 or 5).
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Enumerate UAC configuration:
REG QUERY HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System /v EnableLUA
# EnableLUA = 0x0 <- UAC disabled

REG QUERY HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System /v ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin
# ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin = 0x0 <- auto elevate, no prompt
defense.secure_config:
# Enable UAC at maximum level:
reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System /v EnableLUA /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f
reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System /v ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f

# GPO enforcement:
# Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies
# > Security Options > User Account Control: Run all administrators in Admin Approval Mode = Enabled
defense.evasion: Use a fileless UAC bypass (fodhelper/registry) that self-cleans; remove the added registry keys after elevation.

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Sysmon for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

explain:
Confirms UAC state and level before choosing a bypass:
  REG QUERY HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\ /v EnableLUA   read whether UAC is on
EnableLUA=1 means UAC is active; ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin sets prompt strictness. The OS build number then determines which UAC bypass technique will work.
